Task: Develop a complete lesson plan for teaching probability to high-school students.

High-School Mathematics  
Unit: Introduction to Probability  
Lesson Title: “Predicting the Unpredictable”  
Total Lesson Time: 90 minutes (extendable to block schedule or split into two 45-minute periods)

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Standards & Learning Goals
────────────────────────────────────────
Common Core State Standards (CCSS) – High School Statistics & Probability  
• HSS-CP.A.1: Understand that probability is a number between 0 and 1.  
• HSS-CP.A.2: Understand the outcomes in a sample space.  
• HSS-CP.A.3: Identify events as subsets of a sample space.  
• HSS-CP.A.5: Use basic probability rules, including complementary, addition, and multiplication rules.  
• Mathematical Practice (SMP) 1, 3, 4, 6.  

By the end of the lesson students will be able to:  
1. Describe probability as a measure between 0 and 1.  
2. List the sample space for simple experiments (coin, die, two coins).  
3. Compute experimental (empirical) and theoretical probabilities for single events.  
4. Apply the complement rule (P(Aʹ)=1–P(A)) and simple addition rule for mutually exclusive events.  
5. Communicate reasoning verbally and in writing, using proper probability notation.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Materials & Technology
────────────────────────────────────────
• For each group (3–4 students):  
  – 2 coins, 1 standard 6-sided die, deck of playing cards (optional)  
  – Small whiteboard or chart paper & markers  
  – “Probability Lab Sheet” handout (see Appendix A)  
• Teacher demo: computer + projector with internet; open free simulation (e.g., GeoGebra, PhET, or Desmos “Coin Flip Simulation”).  
• Exit Ticket slips (¼ sheet per student)  
• Colored dot stickers (green, yellow, red) for quick formative check.

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Lesson Flow (90 min)
────────────────────────────────────────
A. Warm-Up / Hook (10 min)  
   1. Display a jar with 3 red and 1 blue marble (physical or image).  
   2. Ask: “If I draw one marble without looking, which color is more likely? Why? Give a percent if you can.”  
   3. Students respond on mini-whiteboards → show.  
   4. Briefly discuss that “likelihood” can be quantified; introduce probability scale 0–1 (or 0–100 %).  

B. Direct Instruction & Concept Building (15 min)  
   1. Definition: Probability = favorable outcomes ÷ total outcomes.  
   2. Key vocabulary: experiment, outcome, event, sample space, theoretical vs experimental probability, complement, mutually exclusive.  
   3. Visualize with number line 0–1: impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely, certain.  
   4. Model Example (teacher led): Rolling a die, P(rolling prime number) = 3/6 = 0.5. Show fraction → decimal → percent.

C. Guided Inquiry – “Probability Stations Lab” (30 min)  
   Students rotate (or stay in groups) through 3 quick experiments, recording both experimental data and theoretical predictions.  

   Station 1 – Two-Coin Toss (10 min)  
   • Predict P(2 heads).  
   • Flip both coins 20 times; record HH, HT, TH, TT tallies.  
   • Compare frequency vs theory (¼).  

   Station 2 – Single Die Roll (10 min)  
   • Predict P(rolling number >4).  
   • Roll 30 times; record counts 1–6; compute relative frequency.  

   Station 3 – Deck Draw (10 min)  
   • Remove jokers. Predict P(drawing a Heart), P(face card).  
   • Shuffle; draw, record, and replace 25 draws.  

   Teacher/TA circulates with probing questions:  
   – “How did you decide on your prediction?”  
   – “What is your sample space?”  
   – “Why might experimental results differ slightly?”  

D. Synthesis & Whole-Class Discussion (10 min)  
   • Each group posts results (chart paper). Class compares.  
   • Highlight Law of Large Numbers—frequencies approach theoretical values as trials increase.  
   • Introduce complement rule: P(A) + P(Aʹ) = 1. Quick example using die or jar.

E. Skill Practice / Application (15 min)  
   Hand out “Practice Set” (differentiated: basic, challenge rows). Students work individually; partner check after 5 min.  
   Sample items:  
   1. What is the probability of drawing a red or a Queen from a standard deck?  
   2. If P(rain) = 0.3 tomorrow, what is P(no rain)?  
   3. Bag with 5 green, 2 yellow, 3 blue candies. a) P(green). b) P(not yellow).  

   Teacher does quick “traffic-light” check with colored stickers on name tents: green = confident, yellow = unsure, red = stop & help.

F. Closure / Exit Ticket (5 min)  
   Prompt: “Describe one thing you learned about probability today and solve: A die is rolled. What is P(odd number OR 6)?”  
   (Answer: 4/6 = 2/3.) Collect.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Assessment
────────────────────────────────────────
Formative  
• Warm-up responses, teacher questions during lab, traffic-light stickers, exit ticket.  
• Observe group discourse for Mathematical Practice 3 (construct & critique arguments).  

Summative (for next class or homework)  
• Problem set covering objectives.  
• Mini-quiz: sample-space listing, complements, simple OR probabilities.  

────────────────────────────────────────
5. Differentiation & Supports
────────────────────────────────────────
• English Learners: Provide vocabulary foldable, sentence frames (“The probability of ___ is ___ because ___.”), pictorial sample spaces.  
• Students with IEP/504: Allow calculator use for division, extra time, seat near front.  
• Early Finishers/Advanced: Challenge task—two-way table of rolling two dice; find P(sum is prime OR even).  
• Struggling Students: Pair with supportive peer; offer manipulatives (colored chips) in practice section.

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Anticipated Misconceptions & Teacher Moves
────────────────────────────────────────
Misconception: Confusing experimental results with theoretical probability.  
Move: Emphasize “short-run variability, long-run stability” via class discussion.  

Misconception: Believing previous outcomes affect independent events (“Gambler’s fallacy”).  
Move: Ask, “Does the coin remember previous flips?” Use simulation to show independence.  

Error: Adding probabilities of non-mutually-exclusive events without subtracting overlap.  
Move: Provide Venn diagram visuals next lesson when intersections are introduced.

────────────────────────────────────────
7. Extension / Next Steps
────────────────────────────────────────
Next lesson: Compound events using tree diagrams & two-way tables; introduce multiplication rule and conditional probability.

Homework (optional tonight):  
• Use an online coin-flip simulator to perform 200 tosses. Paste screenshot of results and answer reflection questions: How close was HH frequency to 25 %? What changed between 20 and 200 trials?

────────────────────────────────────────
Appendix A – Probability Lab Sheet (condensed)

Name: __________ Group: ___  
Experiment | Theoretical P(Event) | # Trials | # Successes | Experimental P  
Two-Coin Toss – 2 Heads | ____ | 20 | ___ | ___  
Die Roll – >4 | ____ | 30 | ___ | ___  
Card Draw – Heart | ____ | 25 | ___ | ___

Reflection: 1) Which experiment showed the greatest difference? 2) Predict what would happen if you doubled the number of trials.

────────────────────────────────────────
Teacher Reflection (post-lesson)
1. What questions elicited the richest discussion?  
2. Did the traffic-light quickly identify misconceptions?  
3. How will I connect today’s ideas to compound probability tomorrow?
